issues.legal_issue: A government allocation of public resources to a private enterprise is valid when its terms are reasonable and serve the public interest rather than confer a private benefit at the State’s expense.
material_facts: The State had adopted a policy of using resin from its forests to encourage industries within the State.
The allocated forest areas were inaccessible, and prior attempts to obtain contractors for tapping them had largely failed; extraction involved high costs and scarce skilled labour.
The selected enterprise had to extract a minimum quantity of resin, surrender a portion to the State, and use the resin it retained only in a factory established within the State.
The arrangement enabled the State to obtain resin for its own use, secure extraction from otherwise unworked areas, and encourage industrial development, employment, and State revenue.
The Court found that the terms did not confer a large benefit on the enterprise at the State’s cost and that the State’s return compared favourably with the costs and alternative arrangements.
issues.conclusion: The allocation was reasonable and in the public interest, and was not shown to benefit the private enterprise at the State’s expense.
issues.legal_principle: Government largess must be granted on reasonable terms and for the public good; State action is invalid if it is unreasonable or lacks public interest, though the State may accept less than the highest possible consideration when other public-interest considerations justify doing so. The court assesses the totality of relevant considerations, presumes governmental action reasonable and in the public interest, and places a heavy burden on the challenger to show otherwise. Reasonableness under Articles 14, 19 and 21 is informed by the Directive Principles. The Court relied on Ramana Dayaram Shetty v. International Airport Authority of India, State of Madras v. V.G. Row, E.P. Royappa v. State of Tamil Nadu, and Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India.

rule.if: constitutional_writ_challenging_state_resource_grant and public_industrial_objective and resource_was_unworkable_under_ordinary_contracts and state_received_substantial_public_benefits and not private_gain_at_state_expense

predicates.constitutional_writ_challenging_state_re: A person brought a constitutional writ challenging a government’s grant of public resources to a private enterprise.
predicates.public_industrial_objective: The government made the grant to advance an industrial-development objective that would benefit the public.
predicates.resource_was_unworkable_under_ordinary_c: The government relied on evidence that the resource could not practically be developed through ordinary contracting arrangements.
predicates.state_received_substantial_public_benefi: The terms gave the State material or economic benefits from the arrangement.
predicates.private_gain_at_state_expense: The grant gave the private recipient a benefit at the State’s expense.

issues.definition: When a constitutional writ challenges a State resource grant, a public industrial objective, practical difficulty with ordinary contracts, and substantial benefits to the State, without a private gain at the State’s expense, lead to the grant surviving reasonableness and public-interest review.

issues.legal_issue: Allocating a limited part of a resource to one enterprise does not create a monopoly or impose an unreasonable restriction on others’ occupational freedom when substantial opportunities remain available to them.
material_facts: The allocation covered blazes in inaccessible forest areas rather than all forest areas in the State.
A substantially larger number of blazes in other forest areas remained available for tapping by other contractors.

One group of petitioners obtained a wage contract for an accessible forest, and the other group’s failure to obtain a contract was attributable to its failure to renew its registration, not to an absence of available blazes.
issues.conclusion: The allocation neither created a monopoly in favour of the selected enterprise nor imposed an unreasonable restriction on the petitioners’ right to carry on tapping business.
issues.legal_principle: Article 19(1)(g) protects the freedom to carry on an occupation, but an allocation does not amount to a monopoly or unreasonable restriction merely because one enterprise receives a defined resource allocation, where other opportunities remain available. State action must also satisfy the non-arbitrariness requirement of Article 14, as explained in E.P. Royappa v. State of Tamil Nadu and Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India.

predicates.constitutional_writ_challenging_state_re: A person brought a constitutional writ challenging a government’s allocation of a resource to an enterprise.
predicates.allocation_was_confined_to_part_of_the_r: The government allocated only a defined portion of the available resource to the enterprise.
predicates.substantial_opportunities_remained_for_o: A substantial amount of the resource remained available for others to pursue comparable work.
predicates.challengers_could_compete_for_remaining_: The challengers were able to seek contracts or other opportunities involving the resources that remained available.

issues.definition: When a constitutional writ challenges a limited resource allocation, and substantial opportunities remain open to challengers who can compete for them, the allocation does not create a monopoly or an unreasonable occupational restriction.

issues.legal_issue: The State may select an enterprise through negotiation without inviting specific tenders when the transaction allocates resources as part of a bona fide, reasonable, and publicly beneficial industrial-development arrangement.
material_facts: The selected enterprise had approached the State with a proposal to establish a resin-processing factory and sought an assured supply of resin for it.
The State’s arrangement linked the resource allocation to the establishment of a factory and restricted use of the retained resin to that factory within the State.
The State considered applicants using financial capacity and experience in resin extraction and processing as relevant criteria.
The selected enterprise had substantial experience in extraction and processing, while the petitioners lacked comparable processing experience.
The State did not invite specific tenders for the allocation, but it had publicly invited entrepreneurs to establish industries and offer proposals for industrial development.
issues.conclusion: The absence of a specific advertisement or tender did not invalidate the selection because the resource allocation was part of a bona fide and reasonable industrial-development arrangement in the public interest.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 14 and the administrative-law rule affirmed in Ramana Dayaram Shetty v. International Airport Authority of India, the State must select recipients of largess fairly and according to a rational, relevant, non-arbitrary standard. The State is not required to invite tenders for a resource allocation made as part of an industrial incentive package, provided its action is bona fide, reasonable, and in the public interest; a straightforward contract to tap resources would ordinarily require auction or tenders to secure the highest price, subject to overriding public-interest considerations. The Court also relied on E.P. Royappa v. State of Tamil Nadu and Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India on non-arbitrariness and reasonableness under Article 14.

rule.if: constitutional_writ_challenging_state_recipient_selection and no_specific_tender_was_invited and resource_allocation_was_part_of_an_industrial_incentive and selection_used_relevant_criteria and state_action_was_bona_fide_and_reasonable

predicates.constitutional_writ_challenging_state_re: A person brought a constitutional writ challenging the State’s selection of a recipient for a public resource or benefit.
predicates.no_specific_tender_was_invited: The State did not invite specific tenders for the challenged allocation.
predicates.resource_allocation_was_part_of_an_indus: The State allocated resources to induce or support the establishment of an industry that served a public objective.
predicates.selection_used_relevant_criteria: The State selected the recipient by applying criteria relevant to the recipient’s ability to carry out the arrangement.
predicates.state_action_was_bona_fide_and_reasonabl: The State acted genuinely and on a reasonable basis rather than from an improper motive or arbitrary preference.

issues.definition: When a constitutional writ challenges a selection made without a specific tender, the absence of a tender does not invalidate the selection if the allocation formed part of an industrial incentive, relevant criteria were applied, and the State acted bona fide and reasonably.
